about: "Make it specific" prompts for unit-5 (docs/aphug-architecture.md, "Make it specific"); checked by checkJustify in scripts/lib/aphug-exams.mjs.

prompts.title: Describing transhumance
prompts.prompt: Describe transhumance as it is practiced in the Swiss Alps.
checklist: Says what moves and where
Says when it moves, by season
Explains it is a yearly pattern, more than a definition

earns.answer: In the Swiss Alps, farmers move cattle up to high mountain pastures in early summer, when the grass grows after the snow melts, and bring them back down to the valley farms in autumn, a seasonal pattern repeated every year.
earns.why: It says what moves, where and when, in a named place.

misses.answer: Transhumance is moving animals to different pastures.
misses.why: A definition with no place and no seasons: describe the pattern itself.

pattern.label: Summer
options: cattle move up to high pastures

why.1: The Alps move up and down, not to the coast.
why.2: Summer is when the high pastures are used.

trend.label: Autumn
options: cattle come back down to the valleys

why.1: Snow comes to the high pastures in autumn.
why.2: They return to the valley farms.

prompts.title: The Columbian Exchange on an Italian plate
prompts.prompt: Explain how the Columbian Exchange changed food in Italy.
checklist: Names a crop and where it came from
Names the process and when it began
Links it to a change in Italian food

earns.answer: Tomatoes came from the Americas to Europe after 1492 through the Columbian Exchange, so by the 1800s they had become central to Italian dishes such as pasta sauces and pizza.
earns.why: It names the crop, its origin, the process and the result.

misses.answer: Italians eat tomatoes because of the Columbian Exchange.
misses.why: It names the process but not where tomatoes came from or how food changed.

why.1: Wheat came from Southwest Asia.
why.2: Rice did not come from Australia.

why.1: Bread stayed central too.
why.2: Tomatoes stayed and spread.

prompts.title: Two agricultural revolutions
prompts.prompt: Compare the Second Agricultural Revolution and the Green Revolution.
checklist: Gives one similarity between the two revolutions
Gives where, when and how for both
Speaks of both revolutions, not one alone

earns.answer: Both raised farm output with new methods, but the Second Agricultural Revolution, in Britain from the 1700s, relied on crop rotation, enclosure and new machines, whereas the Green Revolution, from the 1960s in places such as India and Mexico, relied on high-yield seeds, fertilizers and irrigation.
earns.why: It gives a similarity and a difference, with time, place and method for both.

misses.answer: The Green Revolution used high-yield seeds and fertilizers.
misses.why: One side only: say what the Second Agricultural Revolution did too.

why.1: That is the Green Revolution.
why.2: That is the Columbian Exchange.

why.1: Genetically modified crops came later and are separate.
why.2: That is the earlier revolution.

prompts.title: The Green Revolution in India
prompts.prompt: Explain the degree to which the Green Revolution reduced hunger in India.
checklist: States the degree first: to a large degree, for example
Names the technology and a region, with dates
Names a cost or who gained less

earns.answer: To a large degree: from the late 1960s, high-yield wheat and rice, with irrigation and fertilizer, raised harvests in states such as Punjab, so India no longer faced the famines it had feared; but the gains went most to farmers with water and money, and groundwater fell.
earns.why: It states the degree and backs it with both the gains and the costs.

misses.answer: The Green Revolution fixed hunger in India with new seeds.
misses.why: No degree and an overstatement: the gains were uneven and had costs.

why.1: Harvests rose sharply.
why.2: Gains were uneven, so not complete.

why.1: High-yield seeds were the heart of it.
why.2: Irrigation, not more rain, watered the crops.

prompts.title: Naming a place: commodity dependence
prompts.context: A student writes: "Some countries depend on one crop for their exports."
prompts.prompt: Rewrite the claim with a real country, its crop and why it matters.
checklist: Names a real country and crop, with a dated source
Says what depending on it means
Gives the effect of a price change

earns.answer: Côte d'Ivoire, the world's largest grower of cocoa beans (FAOSTAT, 2022 data), earns a large share of its export income from cocoa, so a fall in world cocoa prices cuts farm incomes and government revenue.
earns.why: It names the country, crop and source, and the effect of a price fall.

misses.answer: Some African countries depend on cocoa or coffee.
misses.why: "Some African countries" names no place, and nothing says why it matters.

why.1: A continent, not a country.
why.2: That names no country.

why.1: Lower prices mean less money.
why.2: Most export income comes from cocoa.

prompts.title: Soybeans at two scales
prompts.prompt: Explain how Brazil's soybean production looks different at the global and local scales.
checklist: Names Brazil's place at the global scale
Names where in Brazil the crop is grown
Explains what that means for the country's output

earns.answer: At the global scale, Brazil is one of the largest exporters of soybeans, but at the local scale, much of the crop comes from large farms in states such as Mato Grosso, so the national total depends on a few regions and the land cleared there.
earns.why: It names both scales and what each shows.

misses.answer: Brazil grows a lot of soybeans and sells them abroad.
misses.why: No scale is named and no place inside Brazil is given.

scale.label: Global scale
options: one of the largest soybean exporters

why.1: Brazil sells soybeans abroad in large amounts.
why.2: Brazil is a major grower.

why.1: Soy comes mostly from large farms.
why.2: Crops grow on land, not in the river.

prompts.title: A limit of von Thünen
prompts.prompt: Explain one limit of the von Thünen model, using a named place.
checklist: Says what the model assumes about transport
Names a real place where the pattern breaks
Explains why modern transport breaks it

earns.answer: Von Thünen assumed one market and travel by horse and cart over flat land, but flowers grown in the Netherlands are flown from Schiphol airport to markets around the world, so modern transport lets perishable goods travel far, which breaks the model's rings.
earns.why: It states the assumption, names a place and explains the break.

misses.answer: The von Thünen model is old, so it does not fit farming in the 2020s.
misses.why: No reason and no place: a limit needs the assumption that fails and a case.

model.label: Assumption
options: travel by horse and cart to one market

why.1: That is the modern world that breaks the model.
why.2: The model has several rings of different crops.

place.label: Where it breaks
options: dairy farms near a market town
grain grown far from a market

why.1: Dairy near a market town fits the model.
why.2: Distant grain fits the model too.

prompts.title: Irrigation and the Aral Sea
prompts.prompt: Explain how irrigated farming changed the Aral Sea in Central Asia.
checklist: Names the farming and the rivers it took water from, with the date
Links the water taken to the sea shrinking
Names an effect on people or land

earns.answer: From the 1960s, Soviet planners took water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton, so less water reached the Aral Sea, which shrank to a fraction of its size, leaving fishing towns far from the shore and salty dust blowing over farms.
earns.why: It names the cause, links it to the shrinking and gives effects.

misses.answer: The Aral Sea dried up because of farming.
misses.why: It names a cause but not how farming took the water or what followed.

why.1: The sea shrank, it did not rise.
why.2: More rain would fill it.

effect.label: Effect
options: fishing towns left far from the shore

why.1: Fishing collapsed as the sea shrank.
why.2: The sea shrank to a fraction of its size.

prompts.title: What farm labor data miss
prompts.context: A national count of workers records each person's main paid job.
prompts.prompt: Explain one limitation of this count for measuring women's work in farming.
checklist: Names what the count misses: unpaid family farm work
Says why women's work is often missed
Says which way the figures are off

earns.answer: Counts of main paid jobs miss much of the unpaid work women do on family farms, such as weeding, harvesting and processing food, so the data can understate women's share of farm labor.
earns.why: It names the gap, gives examples and says which way the figures err.

misses.answer: The count might not include enough women in it.
misses.why: It guesses at sampling but misses the real gap: unpaid work is not counted.

why.1: Paid jobs are what the count records.
why.2: Men's main jobs are recorded.

why.1: Missing work makes the share look smaller.
why.2: Missing work means the data are not exact.

prompts.title: Reading a dot map legend
prompts.context: A dot map of invented Country A shows dairy cows, with a legend that reads "1 dot = 1,000 cows" (invented data for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain what a cluster of 20 dots in one province means, and what it does not mean.
checklist: Reads the value from the legend: about 20,000 cows
Says the dots show where cows are counted
Says a dot is not one farm

earns.answer: With 1 dot standing for 1,000 cows, 20 dots mean about 20,000 cows in that area; the dots show where the cows are counted, not the exact spot of each farm, so one dot may stand for several farms nearby.
earns.why: It reads the legend's value and says what a dot does not show.

misses.answer: There are a lot of cows in that province.
misses.why: It never reads the legend: how many cows do 20 dots stand for?

why.1: Each dot is 1,000 cows, not one.
why.2: Dots count cows, not farms.

limit.label: What a dot is not
options: the exact spot of one farm

why.1: A dot is a count of cows.
why.2: Dots are on the map.
